extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students of literature, and critics interested in classical dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging poetic and dramatic works (especially tragedy, epic, and comedy) based on Aristotle's Poetics: definitions of genre, constituent parts, and principles like unity, plot construction, and catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is the imitation of an action that is serious and also, as having magnitude, complete in itself; in language with pleasurable accessories, each kind brought in separately in the parts of the work; in a dramatic, not in a narrative form; with incidents arousing pity and fear, wherewith to accomplish its catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'language with pleasurable accessories' (rhythm, harmony/song) and that some portions are verse and others song; emphasises dramatic presentation rather than narrative; links purpose to arousing pity and fear to effect catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy has six parts: Plot (Fable), Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, and Melody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part is defined: Plot = combination of incidents (things done); Character = what makes us ascribe moral qualities; Thought = what is said in proving points or asserting universals; Diction = composition of words/verses; Melody = musical element; Spectacle = stage appearance. Notes two arise from the means, one from manner, three from objects; nothing else exists besides these six.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (Action over Character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important of the six is the combination of the incidents of the story: tragedy is primarily an imitation of action and life, and the action (Plot) is the end and purpose of the tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character is subordinate—there may be a tragedy without character but not without action. Peripety and discoveries (reversals/recognitions) are parts of Plot and are powerful elements. Beginners succeed earlier in diction and character than in plot-construction; good diction without a plot fails to produce true tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (Each part subserves the whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work should have unity, so that each part should subserve the whole; irrelevancies, however brilliant, should be cast away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle stresses following the 'natural order' from first principles; a plot must be a unified sequence where incidents relate causally and appear to happen because of one another. Avoid episodic or irrelevant material that does not advance the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and Magnitude of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be 'complete' with a beginning, middle and end, and possess magnitude—an appropriate size or importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness means an integrated whole with necessary causal ties; magnitude implies suitable scale (e.g., tragic action often confined to a single circuit of the sun). Epic differs by greater length due to no fixed time-limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity or Probability of Episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequence of events should be either necessary or probable and 'appear to happen because of one another'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle recommends events be causally connected; improbable or gratuitous incidents weaken the tragic effect. Events should look as if they must or naturally would follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either simple (lacking reversal and recognition) or complex (including peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition), and often pathos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots that use reversal and recognition typically produce stronger tragic effects. Simple plots may still be complete but lack those dramatic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal) and Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia (reversal of fortune) and anagnorisis (recognition/discovery) are key techniques that, when present (often together), powerfully affect the tragic plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle suggests these elements are historically rooted in ritual drama and commonly linked; their joint occurrence is especially effective in arousing pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (Error/Tragic Flaw)
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical tragic hero falls from high state or fame, not through vice or depravity, but by some great hamartia—an error, fault, or mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamartia should be understood broadly (error/offence/‘bad shot’) rather than narrowly as solely moral depravity; the hero is great yet has 'something wrong' that precipitates the fall, eliciting pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must have distinctive qualities of character and thought; they ought to be appropriate, consistent, and make us ascribe moral qualities to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character exists for the sake of action; tragedy can be without character but not without action. Character reveals moral purpose; speeches on indifferent subjects do not serve character. Good characters should fit their parts and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Ideas and Argument in Speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the power of saying whatever can be said or is appropriate to the occasion—shown in speech when proving a point or enunciating a general truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought is distinct from character; it aligns with rhetoric and political discourse. The older poets make characters speak like statesmen; moderns like rhetoricians. Thought should be suited to the circumstances and contribute to plot and moral implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Language (Composition of Verses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction denotes the composition of the verses—the expression of thoughts in words; language (including metre and rhythm) is a central means of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of metre (iambic vs trochaic, hexameter etc.) matters; 'language with pleasurable accessories' refers to rhythm and harmony. Diction must be appropriate to character and occasion; verse vs prose effects differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody and Musical Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (song) is the greatest of the pleasurable accessories of tragedy and an important element of its appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melody should be integrated into the parts where appropriate. It is part of the means of imitation alongside diction and contributes to the aesthetic pleasure of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Visual/Staging Elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (stage-appearance of actors, visual effects) must be some part of the whole, but it is the least artistic element and has the least to do with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic effect is possible without public performance; spectacle is more a matter for costumier/producer than poet. It attracts but is not the core poetic craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: Catharsis of Pity and Fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy uses incidents arousing pity and fear in order to accomplish a catharsis (purification/purgation) of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle links catharsis possibly to ritual purification; the dramatic arousal and resolution of passions serve a communal/psychological function. The poet should craft incidents that properly trigger and resolve these emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Subject Matter (Great Life, Noble Themes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great art must have for its subject the great way of living; each form of art should produce its proper pleasure and engage proper subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical view: tragedy treats serious, noble actions; comedy imitates the low or ridiculous. Choice of subject should suit the genre's proper aim and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means, Objects, and Manner as Genre-Differentiators
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic/dramatic arts differ by (I) their means (rhythm, language, harmony), (II) the objects they imitate (actions by agents above, below, or like us), and (III) their manner (narration vs assumed character vs full dramatic enactment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of rhythm/harmony/voice and whether imitation is by narrative or enactment distinguishes epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyramb, etc. Genre classification should be grounded in these three heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Comedy and the Ridiculous
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of men worse than the average; the Ridiculous is a species of the Ugly defined as a mistake or deformity not productive of pain or harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy aims at the ridiculous (harmless deformity), historically tied to invective and iambic metre; masks etc. are used to excite laughter without causing harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: Form and Constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry agrees with tragedy as an imitation of serious subjects in a grand kind of verse but differs in being narrative, in one kind of verse (hexameter), and in length—it has no fixed time limit, whereas tragedy tries to keep to a single circuit of the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While all parts of an epic are included in tragedy, not all tragic parts belong to epic. A judge of tragedy can judge epic too because of shared constituents, but the forms and constraints differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development and Natural Form of Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of art grow and develop until they 'attain their natural form'; poetry originated from imitation and rhythm and improved gradually from improvisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/technical changes (e.g., increase in actors, use of scenery, shift of metres) are part of a genre's maturation; producers should be aware of both tradition and the natural limits of a form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical Language Sensitivity (Word-meaning and Translation Issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key Greek terms (e.g., poesis/poetes as 'making/maker', hamartia, praxis, katharsis) have nuanced meanings and translations influence theoretical interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners/readers should be cautious when importing modern senses; understanding original semantic range (e.g., hamartia as 'error' not only 'moral flaw') affects how one composes and evaluates character and action.
